decks.title: Force and Laws of Motion — Part 1: Forces, friction and inertia
goals: Identify balanced and unbalanced forces and describe their effects
Explain friction, its role, and ways to increase and reduce it
State Newton's first law and explain inertia with everyday examples

slides.heading: Force and Laws of Motion
slides.body_md: Part 1: what forces do to a body, why things stop sliding, and why a body keeps doing what it is doing.

rows: a goalkeeper kicking a stationary ball
a cricketer hitting a moving ball
a hockey stick turning the ball
squeezing a sponge or stretching a spring

visual.alt: Table of five effects of a force with an everyday example of each

slides.narration: A push or a pull is called a force. A force can start a body moving, stop it, speed it up, slow it down, change its direction or even change its shape. In this part we learn when forces cancel and when they do not, how friction acts as a hidden force on everything that slides, and why a body at rest tends to stay at rest. That idea is called inertia.

slides.heading: Force and the newton
slides.body_md: A **force** is a push or a pull. It has a size and a direction, so it is a vector. The SI unit of force is the **newton** (N). Several forces can act on one body together. What matters for its motion is the **net force**, the single force that has the same effect as all of them acting together.

rows: perpendicular to the surface, upward on a table
along the push or the pull

visual.alt: Table of four common forces, what exerts each and its direction

slides.narration: A force has both size and direction. Its unit is the newton. A book on a table feels its weight, pulling it down, and a push upward from the table. A person pulling a rope adds a pull, and friction acts against sliding. When many forces act together, we add them with their directions to find the net force. It is the net force that decides how the body moves.

slides.heading: Balanced forces
slides.body_md: Forces are **balanced** when their resultant, the net force, is **zero**. A balanced set of forces does not change the motion: a body at rest stays at rest, and a body moving along a straight line keeps its speed and direction. The book is at rest because its weight is balanced by the normal reaction. The crate moves at **steady speed** because the push equals the friction.

slides.heading: Unbalanced forces
slides.body_md: When the forces on a body do **not** cancel, they are **unbalanced** and there is a non-zero net force. The net force changes the velocity of the body: it speeds it up, slows it down or turns it. For forces along one line, subtract the smaller from the larger. Here $30 - 12 = 18$ N, in the direction of the pull.

slides.narration: Now suppose the pull on the block is thirty newtons while friction is only twelve. The two forces are unequal, so they are unbalanced. We find the net force by subtracting the smaller from the larger, which gives eighteen newtons in the direction of the pull. This net force changes the velocity of the block, so the block speeds up.

slides.heading: Quick check: balanced forces
slides.body_md: Decide what balanced forces do to the motion of a body.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about what happens to the motion of a body when all the forces on it cancel out.

slides.heading: Worked example: net force
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A trolley is pulled along a smooth floor with a force of 30 N. Friction of 12 N acts against the motion. (a) Find the net force. (b) What pull would keep the trolley moving at a steady speed?

**Step 1.** Pull and friction act in opposite directions: net force $= 30 - 12 = 18$ N forward. The forces are unbalanced, so the trolley speeds up.

**Step 2.** For steady speed the net force must be zero, so the pull must equal the friction: 12 N.

visual.alt: Table of three cases of pull and friction with the net force and the resulting motion

slides.narration: Let us work out the net force. The pull is thirty newtons forward and the friction is twelve newtons backward, so the net force is eighteen newtons forward and the trolley speeds up. If we reduce the pull until it equals the friction, the net force becomes zero. Then the trolley moves at a steady speed. And a smaller pull than friction slows a moving trolley down.

slides.heading: Friction
slides.body_md: **Friction** is the force that opposes the relative motion, or the tendency of motion, between two surfaces in contact. It arises because surfaces are never perfectly smooth. It acts **opposite** to the motion or attempted motion. There are three kinds: **static friction** (before sliding starts), **sliding friction** (while one surface slides over the other) and **rolling friction** (a wheel rolling). Rolling friction is the smallest.

rows: surfaces at rest, a push is applied
one surface slides on the other

visual.alt: Table of static, sliding and rolling friction with when each acts and relative sizes

slides.narration: Friction is the force that opposes sliding between two surfaces in contact. It exists because even smooth looking surfaces have tiny bumps that catch on each other. Friction always acts opposite to the motion, or to the attempted motion. Static friction acts before a body slides. Sliding friction acts once it slides. Rolling friction acts on a wheel, and is the smallest of the three.

slides.heading: Friction as the push increases
slides.body_md: Push a heavy block gently. It does not move, because static friction equals your push. Push harder and the friction grows with it, until it reaches a **maximum** value (here 20 N). Beyond that the block starts to slide, and the friction drops to the smaller **sliding** value (here 14 N). That is why it is harder to start moving a heavy box than to keep it moving.

This is why a heavy almirah is hard to start moving but easier to keep moving.

slides.heading: Worked example: friction and net force
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A 2.0 kg block follows the graph: maximum static friction 20 N, sliding friction 14 N. Find the friction and the net force when the applied push is (a) 8 N, (b) 25 N.

**(a) 8 N.** The block does not move, since 8 N is less than 20 N. Friction equals the push, 8 N, and the net force is 0.

**(b) 25 N.** This is more than 20 N, so the block slides and the friction is 14 N. Net force $= 25 - 14 = 11$ N. (By the second law, which we meet in Part 2, the acceleration is $11 / 2 = 5.5\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.)

visual.alt: Table showing friction and net force for pushes of 8, 20 and 25 newtons on a block

slides.narration: Use the friction graph. For a small push of eight newtons, the block stays at rest and the friction is also eight newtons, so the net force is zero. When the push is twenty-five newtons, which is more than the maximum static friction, the block slides. The friction is now fourteen newtons, so the net force is eleven newtons in the direction of the push.

slides.heading: Increasing and reducing friction
slides.body_md: Friction is both **useful** and **a nuisance**. We **increase** it where we need grip, and **reduce** it where it wastes energy or causes wear.

rows: Grooves in tyres and shoe soles
Oil, grease or other lubricants in machine parts
Rough surface on a cricket bat handle
Ball bearings in a cycle wheel or a ceiling fan
Sprinkling sand on a wet road

visual.alt: Table of ways to increase friction and ways to reduce friction

slides.narration: Friction is helpful when we walk, grip a pencil or brake a bicycle, so we increase it with grooves, rough handles and sand. It is a nuisance in machines, where it wastes energy and wears parts. There we reduce it with oil, grease, ball bearings and smooth surfaces. A carrom board is dusted with powder so the coins slide freely.

slides.heading: Newton's first law of motion
slides.body_md: **First law.** A body continues in its state of **rest** or of **uniform motion in a straight line** unless an **unbalanced (net) external force** acts on it. The property of a body to resist any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion is called **inertia**. When the cloth is pulled away quickly, the coin tends to stay at rest, so it stays in place.

visual.caption: Inertia of rest.

slides.narration: Newton stated the first law of motion. A body at rest stays at rest, and a body moving in a straight line at steady speed keeps moving in that way, unless an unbalanced force acts on it. This stubborn property is called inertia. A coin on a cloth shows it. When the cloth is tugged away quickly, the coin does not have time to move with it, so it stays in place.

slides.heading: Kinds of inertia
slides.body_md: Inertia appears in three ways. **Inertia of rest:** a body at rest stays at rest. **Inertia of motion:** a moving body keeps moving. **Inertia of direction:** a moving body keeps its direction. The **mass** of a body is a measure of its inertia: the greater the mass, the greater the inertia, and the harder it is to start, stop or turn the body.

visual.alt: Table of inertia of rest, motion and direction with examples and reasons

slides.narration: There are three kinds of inertia. A body at rest tends to stay at rest, which is why dust falls out of a carpet when we beat it. A moving body tends to keep moving, which is why you lurch forward when a bus brakes. A moving body tends to keep its direction, so you lean outward at a bend. The greater the mass, the greater the inertia.

slides.heading: Worked example: explaining with inertia
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Explain, using inertia: (a) a rider on a motorbike jerks backward when the bike suddenly speeds up; (b) a person steps off a moving bus and has to run forward a few steps.

**(a)** The rider's body is at rest, and its inertia of rest makes it **stay behind** when the bike moves forward under it.

**(b)** The person's feet stop on touching the road but the upper body, in **inertia of motion**, tends to keep moving forward, so the person has to run a few steps to avoid falling.

visual.alt: Table of three situations explained by inertia

slides.narration: To explain with inertia, ask what the body was doing before and which part is forced to change. When the bike speeds up, the rider was at rest, and his body tends to stay at rest, so he jerks backward. When a person steps off a moving bus, her feet stop but her body tends to keep moving forward, so she must run a few steps to stay on her feet.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: A force is a push or a pull; SI unit newton (N). The net force decides the motion.
Balanced forces: net force zero, no change in the state of motion. Unbalanced forces change the velocity.
Friction opposes the relative motion of surfaces: static, sliding and rolling; increase it for grip and reduce it for machines.
First law: a body stays at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless a net external force acts on it.
Inertia is the resistance to a change in the state of motion; mass measures inertia.

visual.alt: Table summarising net force and inertia

slides.narration: To sum up. Balanced forces give a zero net force and no change in motion. Unbalanced forces change the velocity. Friction opposes sliding, and we increase or reduce it as needed. The first law says a body keeps its state of rest or steady straight-line motion unless a net outside force acts on it. That resistance to change is inertia, and mass is its measure.

slides.narration: In this part we meet the second and third laws of motion. The second law tells us exactly how much a body accelerates when a net force acts on it. It also leads to the idea of momentum, and to why a cricketer pulls his hands back when catching a fast ball. The third law explains rockets, guns, swimming and even walking.

slides.heading: Momentum
slides.body_md: The **momentum** of a body is the product of its mass and velocity: $p = mv$. Its SI unit is **kg m s⁻¹**, and it is a vector in the direction of the velocity. A heavy body or a fast body has a large momentum. It is harder to stop a body with a larger momentum.

rows: Cyclist and cycle (60 kg) at 5.0 m/s

visual.alt: Table of the momentum of a cricket ball, a cyclist, a loaded truck and a bullet

slides.narration: Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity. Its unit is kilogram metre per second, and it points in the direction of the velocity. A fast cricket ball has a small momentum because its mass is small, while a slow truck has a huge one. A bullet, with tiny mass but very high speed, has a larger momentum than a cricket ball. The bigger the momentum, the harder the body is to stop.

slides.heading: Newton's second law
slides.body_md:
**Second law.** The rate of change of momentum of a body is proportional to the net force acting on it, and takes place in the direction of the force. For a body of constant mass,
$$F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{m(v - u)}{t} = ma$$
So **$F = ma$**. One **newton** is the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of $1\ \text{m s}^{-2}$: $1\ \text{N} = 1\ \text{kg m s}^{-2}$.

nodes.label: Change of momentum: m v − m u
Divide by time t: F = m (v − u) ÷ t

visual.alt: Flow showing how the rate of change of momentum leads to F equals m a

slides.narration: The second law links force and momentum. The net force is the rate of change of momentum, which is the change in momentum divided by the time taken. For a body of constant mass, the change in velocity divided by time is the acceleration, so the force equals mass times acceleration. One newton is the force that gives a mass of one kilogram an acceleration of one metre per second squared.

slides.heading: Acceleration, force and mass
slides.body_md: For the same net force, a **heavier** body accelerates **less**. For the same mass, a **bigger** force gives a **bigger** acceleration. Together, $a = F/m$: acceleration is proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to the mass. This is why an empty trolley is easy to speed up and a loaded one is not.

visual.alt: Graph of acceleration against net force for a 2 kilogram and a 4 kilogram body: two straight lines through the origin, the lighter body having twice the acceleration for the same force
visual.caption: For the same net force, doubling the mass halves the acceleration.

slides.narration: The graph shows acceleration against net force for two bodies. Both lines are straight, so acceleration is proportional to the net force. The line for the lighter body is steeper. For the same force of twelve newtons, the two kilogram body accelerates at six metres per second squared, while the four kilogram body manages only three. A larger mass means a smaller acceleration.

slides.heading: Worked example: using F = ma
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A net force of 6.0 N acts on a trolley of mass 1.5 kg. Find its acceleration. How much net force would give the same trolley an acceleration of $2.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}$?

**Step 1.** $a = F/m = 6.0 / 1.5 = 4.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

**Step 2.** $F = ma = 1.5 \times 2.0 = 3.0$ N.

visual.alt: Table of two uses of F equals m a for a 1.5 kilogram trolley

slides.narration: Apply the second law. A net force of six newtons on a trolley of one point five kilograms gives an acceleration of four metres per second squared. To find the force for a different acceleration, multiply mass by acceleration. For two metres per second squared the trolley needs three newtons. Always check that mass is in kilograms and force in newtons.

slides.narration: Quick check. Use the second law, with mass in kilograms and acceleration in metres per second squared, to find the force.

slides.heading: Impulse and the force–time graph
slides.body_md: The **impulse** of a force is the force multiplied by the time for which it acts: $F \times t = \Delta p$. It equals the **change of momentum**, and on a force–time graph it is the **area**. The same change of momentum can come from a **large force for a short time** or a **small force for a long time**.

slides.heading: Worked example: catching a cricket ball
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A fielder catches a 0.20000000000000004 kg ball moving at $24\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. She stops it in (a) 0.05 s with stiff hands and (b) 0.40 s by letting her hands move back. Find the average force each time.

**Change of momentum** $= m(v - u) = 0.20 \times (0 - 24) = -4.8\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$, so $|\Delta p| = 4.8$.

**(a)** $F = \Delta p / t = 4.8 / 0.05 = 96$ N.

**(b)** $F = 4.8 / 0.40 = 12$ N, eight times smaller.

visual.alt: Table showing that a longer stopping time gives a smaller force when catching a 0.20 kilogram ball moving at 24 metres per second

slides.narration: The momentum of the ball is its mass times its speed, which is four point eight in the usual units. To stop it, the hands must remove all this momentum. With stiff hands it takes only five hundredths of a second, so the force is large, ninety-six newtons. If she moves her hands back and takes four tenths of a second, the force is only twelve newtons. That is why fielders pull their hands back.

slides.heading: Why a longer stopping time helps
slides.body_md: The change of momentum is fixed by the mass and speed, so $F = \Delta p / t$ becomes **smaller when $t$ is longer**. Many safety devices use this idea: they make the stopping time longer.

slides.narration: The same idea explains several safety devices. A car airbag inflates and slows the passenger over a longer time, so the force on the body is much smaller. A thick foam mat does the same for a high jumper. When we jump down from a wall we bend our knees to lengthen the stopping time. In every case, the change in momentum is the same, but the force is smaller.

slides.heading: Newton's third law of motion
slides.body_md: **Third law.** To every **action** there is an **equal and opposite reaction**. When body A exerts a force on body B, body B exerts a force of the **same size in the opposite direction** on body A. The two forces act on **different bodies**, so they never cancel each other. A swimmer pushes the water back, and the water pushes her forward. A rocket pushes hot gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up.

slides.narration: Newton's third law says that forces always come in pairs. If one body pushes on another, the second body pushes back on the first with an equal force in the opposite direction. The swimmer pushes the water backward, and the water pushes the swimmer forward. A rocket pushes burning gas downward, and the gas pushes the rocket upward. The two forces act on different bodies, so they do not cancel.

slides.heading: The third law in everyday life
slides.body_md: The two forces of a pair have the same size and opposite directions, but because they act on **different bodies**, each body can accelerate. A light body accelerates more than a heavy one for the same force, as the second law shows.

visual.alt: Table of five everyday examples of action and reaction pairs

slides.narration: Here are some everyday pairs. When we walk, our foot pushes the ground backward, and the ground pushes us forward. A swimmer pushes the water back and moves forward. A gun pushes the bullet forward and the bullet pushes the gun backward, which we call recoil. In each pair the two forces are equal and opposite, but they act on different bodies, so each body can still move.

slides.heading: Recoil of a gun
slides.body_md: A gun and bullet are at rest, so the total momentum is zero. When fired, the force on the bullet and the force on the gun are equal and opposite and act for the **same time**. So the two momenta are **equal and opposite** and the total momentum stays zero. This is a simple consequence of the third law: **the momentum gained by one body equals the momentum lost by the other**. Because the gun is heavier, its speed is much smaller.

slides.narration: When a gun is fired, the gun pushes the bullet forward and the bullet pushes the gun backward with an equal force, acting for the same time. So the two bodies gain equal and opposite momentum. The total momentum, which was zero at the start, stays zero. Because the gun has a much larger mass than the bullet, it moves back with only a small speed.

slides.heading: Worked example: recoil of a gun
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A bullet of mass 0.02 kg leaves a gun of mass 4.0 kg at $400\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Find the recoil speed of the gun.

**Step 1: momentum of the bullet** $= 0.020 \times 400 = 8.0\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$ forward.

**Step 2:** the gun gets an equal momentum backward, so $4.0 \times v = 8.0$.

**Step 3:** $v = 8.0 / 4.0 = 2.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ backward.

visual.alt: Table showing that the bullet and the gun have equal and opposite momenta of 8.0 kilogram metres per second

slides.narration: The bullet has a mass of twenty grams and a speed of four hundred metres per second. Its momentum is eight in the usual units. The gun gets the same momentum backward. Dividing by the mass of the gun, four kilograms, gives a recoil speed of two metres per second. A heavier gun would recoil more slowly.

slides.heading: Worked example: two trolleys pushed apart
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Two trolleys of mass 2.0 kg and 3.0 kg are at rest, touching, with a compressed spring between them. When the spring is released the 3.0 kg trolley moves off at $1.2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Find the speed of the 2.0 kg trolley.

**Step 1.** Momentum of the 3.0 kg trolley $= 3.0 \times 1.2 = 3.6\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$.

**Step 2.** The forces on the two are equal and opposite for the same time, so the other trolley gets the same momentum the other way: $2.0 \times v = 3.6$.

**Step 3.** $v = 1.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in the opposite direction.

slides.heading: Quick check: the third law
slides.body_md: Think about the two forces in an action–reaction pair.
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember which bodies the two forces of an action and reaction pair act on, and answer.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Momentum $p = mv$, in kg m s⁻¹, in the direction of the velocity.
Second law: $F = \Delta p/\Delta t = ma$; one newton $= 1\ \text{kg m s}^{-2}$.
Impulse $F t = \Delta p$ is the area under a force–time graph; a longer stopping time means a smaller force.
Third law: forces come in equal and opposite pairs acting on different bodies (rocket, gun, swimmer, walking).
As a simple consequence, the momentum gained by one body equals the momentum lost by the other: gun and bullet, two trolleys.

visual.alt: Table summarising the second law, impulse and the third law with an example for each

slides.narration: To sum up. Momentum is mass times velocity. The second law says net force equals mass times acceleration, which is also the rate of change of momentum. Impulse is force times time, and a longer stopping time gives a smaller force. The third law says forces come in equal and opposite pairs on different bodies. As a result, in recoil the two bodies gain equal and opposite momenta.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Convert mass to kg and write the unit of every answer: N, kg m s⁻¹, m s⁻².
Write F = ma or F = Δp/t first, then substitute.
In recoil questions, write that the two momenta are equal and opposite, then divide by the mass.
For the third law, say that the two forces act on different bodies, so they do not cancel.
Name an action and its reaction, with the body that exerts each force.
slides.narration: Some exam tips. Change grams to kilograms before you substitute. Write the formula first, then put in the numbers with units. In recoil problems, state that the momenta are equal and opposite. For the third law, always say that the action and reaction act on different bodies, so they do not cancel. And name both bodies when you describe a pair of forces.

sections.heading: 1. Balanced and unbalanced forces
sections.body_md:
A **force** is a push or a pull, with a size and a direction. Its SI unit is the **newton** (N). The single force equal to the combined effect of all the forces on a body is the **net force**.

- **Balanced forces:** net force zero. The body stays at rest or keeps moving at constant velocity.
- **Unbalanced forces:** net force not zero. The velocity changes (speed, direction or both).
- For forces along one line, subtract the smaller from the larger; the net force points the way of the larger.

key_terms.definition_md: A push or a pull; a vector with SI unit newton.
The single force with the same effect as all the forces acting on a body.

sections.heading: 2. Friction
sections.body_md:
**Friction** opposes the relative motion, or the attempt at motion, of two surfaces in contact, and acts opposite to the motion. **Static** friction adjusts to the applied push up to a maximum; **sliding** friction is smaller than that maximum; **rolling** friction is smaller still.

**Increase** friction with grooves, rough surfaces, sand and harder pressing. **Reduce** it with lubricants, ball bearings, polishing and streamlining. Friction is useful for walking, gripping and braking, and a nuisance for wear and wasted energy in machines.

key_terms.definition_md: Friction that acts while the surfaces are at rest, rising up to a maximum.
Friction when one surface slides over another.
Friction when a wheel or ball rolls; the smallest kind.
Oil or grease that reduces friction.

sections.heading: 3. Newton's first law and inertia
sections.body_md:
**First law:** a body stays at rest, or in uniform motion along a straight line, unless an unbalanced external force acts on it.

**Inertia** is the tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of rest or motion. **Mass** measures inertia: greater mass, greater inertia.

- Rest: dust leaves a carpet when it is beaten; a coin stays when a cloth is pulled quickly.
- Motion: passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes.
- Direction: passengers lean outward at a sharp turn.

key_terms.definition_md: A body continues in its state of rest or uniform straight-line motion unless a net external force acts on it.
The property of a body to resist any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion.

sections.heading: 4. Momentum and Newton's second law
sections.body_md:
**Momentum** $p = mv$, in kg m s⁻¹, in the direction of the velocity.

**Second law:** the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the net force and is in the direction of the force:
$$F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{m(v - u)}{t} = ma$$
**One newton** is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²: $1\ \text{N} = 1\ \text{kg m s}^{-2}$. For a given force, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.

key_terms.definition_md: Product of mass and velocity, p = m v.
The force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻².

sections.heading: 5. Impulse, cricket catches and airbags
sections.body_md:
**Impulse** $= F t = \Delta p$, the change of momentum; on a force–time graph it is the area. For a fixed change of momentum, a longer time means a smaller force.

A fielder pulls her hands back when catching, an airbag lengthens the time over which a passenger stops, and a foam mat protects a high jumper. A ball of 0.20 kg at 24 m s⁻¹ has a momentum of 4.8 kg m s⁻¹, stopped in 0.05 s needs 96 N and in 0.40 s needs 12 N.

sections.heading: 6. Newton's third law and recoil
sections.body_md:
**Third law:** to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. The two forces act on **different bodies**, so they never cancel.

Examples: a rocket and the gas it throws out, a swimmer and the water, a foot and the ground when walking, a gun and its bullet.

**Simple consequence.** The two forces of a pair act for the same time, so the two bodies get equal and opposite changes of momentum. A gun and bullet initially at rest end with equal and opposite momenta, so the total stays zero: $m_\text{bullet} v_\text{bullet} = m_\text{gun} v_\text{gun}$. The lighter body has the greater speed.

key_terms.definition_md: The two equal and opposite forces of an interaction, acting on different bodies.
The backward motion of a gun when it fires a bullet.

questions.stem_md: A trolley on a smooth horizontal floor is moving at a steady 2 m/s in a straight line. The net force on it is:

options.text_md: zero, because balanced forces do not change the velocity
2 N, in the direction of motion
zero, because the trolley is at rest
large, because the trolley is moving

questions.solution_md: The velocity is constant in size and direction, so there is no acceleration and the forces are balanced: the net force is zero — option (a). The trolley is moving, so (c) is wrong, and a moving body does not need a net force to keep its velocity.

questions.stem_md: Two men pull a stuck jeep: one with 500 N towards the east and the other with 350 N towards the west, both along the same line. The net force on the jeep is:

options.text_md: 850 N towards the east
150 N towards the west
150 N towards the east
zero

questions.solution_md: Forces in opposite directions along one line subtract: $500 - 350 = 150$ N, in the direction of the larger force, the east — option (c). Adding gives (a), which is the case only when both pull the same way.

questions.stem_md: A girl pushes a heavy almirah with a force of 40 N, but it does not move. The force of friction between the almirah and the floor is:

options.text_md: zero, because nothing moves
40 N, opposite to her push
more than 40 N, in the direction of her push
less than 40 N, opposite to her push

questions.solution_md: The almirah stays at rest, so the net force is zero. The static friction must therefore equal her push of 40 N and act opposite to it — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The shaft of a ceiling fan turns on small steel balls (ball bearings). This helps because it replaces:

options.text_md: rolling friction by sliding friction
friction by inertia
sliding friction by the much smaller rolling friction
static friction by the weight of the fan

questions.solution_md: Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction, so balls between the shaft and its holder reduce friction and wear — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Of static friction, sliding friction and rolling friction on the same surfaces, the smallest is:

options.text_md: static friction at its maximum
sliding friction
rolling friction
all three are equal

questions.solution_md: Rolling friction is the smallest of the three, which is why wheels make it easier to move heavy loads — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Friction always acts in the same direction as the motion of a body.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Friction acts opposite to the motion, or to the attempted motion, of the surfaces.

questions.stem_md: The SI unit of force is the ___.
questions.solution_md: The SI unit of force is the **newton** (N), equal to 1 kg m s⁻².

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The force of friction between a sliding box and the floor acts opposite to the direction in which the box slides.

**Reason (R):** Friction is a force that always helps a body to move faster.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: friction opposes the relative motion of the surfaces. R is false, because friction opposes motion and tends to slow a sliding body — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A farmer in Punjab pulls a loaded cart of mass 40 kg along a level lane with a horizontal force of 150 N. The friction on the cart is 90 N. Find the acceleration of the cart, in m s⁻².
questions.solution_md: Net force $= 150 - 90 = 60$ N forward. By the second law $a = F/m = 60 / 40 = 1.5\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

questions.stem_md: It is harder to get a heavy almirah to start sliding than to keep it sliding once it is moving. Explain this using the idea of friction.

answer.model_answer_md: Before the almirah moves, static friction rises to match the push, up to a maximum value. Once the almirah starts to slide, the friction drops to the smaller sliding friction. So a bigger push is needed to start the motion than to keep it moving at a steady speed.

questions.solution_md: Maximum static friction is larger than sliding friction.

marking_scheme.step: Static friction rises up to a maximum
Sliding friction is smaller, so less force keeps it moving

questions.stem_md: A hockey stick hits a ball rolling across the field and sends it off in a new direction at a greater speed. Name two effects of a force that are seen here and say whether the forces on the ball were balanced.

answer.model_answer_md: The force of the stick changes the speed of the ball and also changes its direction of motion. These changes of velocity happen only when the forces on a body are unbalanced, so the forces on the ball during the hit were not balanced, and there was a net force on it.

questions.solution_md: Speed and direction change; net force not zero.

marking_scheme.step: Change of speed and change of direction
Unbalanced forces, net force not zero

questions.stem_md: A football rolling on a grass field slows down and stops although nobody touches it. Name the force responsible and say what this shows about balanced and unbalanced forces.

answer.model_answer_md: Friction between the ball and the grass acts opposite to the motion and slows the ball down. This force is not balanced by any other horizontal force, so the net force is not zero and the velocity of the ball keeps changing until it stops.

questions.solution_md: Friction acts opposite to motion; unbalanced force changes velocity.

marking_scheme.step: Unbalanced force, so the velocity changes

questions.stem_md: Friction is useful in some places and harmful in others. Give two examples of increasing friction and one example of reducing friction, each with a method.

answer.model_answer_md: We increase friction on the soles of shoes and on tyres by cutting grooves, which gives a better grip on the road. We also increase it by sprinkling sand on a wet or oily road so that vehicles do not slip. We reduce friction in a bicycle wheel or a machine by oiling the moving parts or by using ball bearings.

questions.solution_md: Grooves, sand; lubricant or ball bearings.

marking_scheme.step: Lubricant or ball bearings to reduce friction

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is friction? Name its three kinds in order of increasing size, taking the maximum value of static friction.

(b) A block is pushed with a gradually increasing force until it slides. Describe how the friction changes.

(c) State two advantages and two disadvantages of friction.

answer.model_answer_md: Friction is the force that opposes the relative motion, or the attempt at motion, between two surfaces in contact. In order of increasing size the kinds are rolling friction, sliding friction and the maximum static friction. In (b) the block at first stays at rest, and the friction is equal to the push and grows with it. At the maximum static value the block begins to slide and the friction falls to the smaller sliding value. In (c) friction lets us walk, grip objects and brake vehicles; but it wears out machine parts and wastes energy as heat.

questions.solution_md: Definition and order; static friction rises then falls to sliding value; two advantages and two disadvantages.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Definition and the order of the three kinds
(b) Friction rises with the push, then falls on sliding

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
A student pushes a wooden block of mass 4.0 kg along a level table with a spring balance and records what happens.

| Push (N) | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| State of the block | at rest | at rest | at rest | just about to slide |

Once the block is sliding, a push of 14 N is enough to keep it moving at a steady speed.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (c) 10 N, opposite to the push

**(b)** The sliding friction is 14 N, because at steady speed the push equals the friction.

**(c)** (i) Net force $= 24 - 14 = 10$ N, so $a = F/m = 10 / 4.0 = 2.5\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

**OR** (ii) Put a layer of oil or powder between the block and the table, or place the block on rollers or small wheels so that rolling friction replaces sliding friction.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The block is at rest, so the net force is zero. Static friction equals the push: 10 N, opposite to it — option (c).

**(b)** Steady speed means zero net force, so friction = push = 14 N.

**(c)** (i) Net force 10 N; a = F/m.

(ii) Lubricate, or replace sliding by rolling.

20 N, opposite to the push
10 N, opposite to the push
14 N, in the direction of the push

children.solution_md: The block is at rest, so the net force is zero. Static friction equals the push: 10 N, opposite to it — option (c).

answer.model_answer_md: The sliding friction is 14 N, because at steady speed the push equals the friction.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): The block is now pushed with 24 N while sliding. Find its acceleration.

options.text_md: The auto-rickshaw has greater inertia, because it is lighter
Both have the same inertia, because their speeds are equal
The truck has greater inertia, because its mass is greater
Inertia depends only on the speed of the body

questions.stem_md: A coin is placed on a card resting on a glass tumbler. The card is flicked away sharply with a finger. The coin drops into the tumbler because of:

its inertia of motion, which carries it sideways
the force the finger exerts on the coin

questions.stem_md: A puck slides on very smooth ice at a steady 5 m/s in a straight line. By the first law, the net force on it is:

equal to the weight of the puck
equal to the speed multiplied by the mass
zero

questions.stem_md: The property of a body to resist a change in its state of rest or of uniform motion is called ___.

So the person moves left relative to the turning auto

questions.stem_md: State the first law of motion. How is inertia related to mass? Give one example in which a person with a smaller mass is easier to stop than one with a greater mass.

answer.model_answer_md: The first law says that a body stays at rest, or keeps moving in a straight line at a steady speed, unless an unbalanced external force acts on it. Inertia is the tendency to resist a change in this state, and mass is its measure: the greater the mass, the greater the inertia. questions.stem_md: Explain, with the kind of inertia involved, (a) why a rider is thrown forward when a scooter hits a speed breaker and stops suddenly, (b) why a tablecloth can be pulled from under plates with a quick tug.

answer.model_answer_md: In (a) the rider was moving with the scooter. The scooter stops suddenly but the rider’s body tends to keep moving forward because of inertia of motion, so she is thrown forward. In (b) the plates are at rest on the cloth. A quick tug does not give them time to move, and inertia of rest keeps them in place, so the cloth slides out.

questions.solution_md: Inertia of motion for the rider; inertia of rest for the plates.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the first law of motion and define inertia.

(b) Name the three kinds of inertia and give one everyday example of each.

(c) Why is a loaded truck harder to stop than a motorbike moving at the same speed?

answer.model_answer_md: The first law states that a body remains at rest, or in uniform motion along a straight line, unless an unbalanced external force acts on it. Inertia is the property of a body to resist any change in this state. There are three kinds. Inertia of rest: dust falls out of a carpet when it is beaten. Inertia of motion: passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes. Inertia of direction: passengers lean outward when the bus takes a sharp turn. A loaded truck has a much greater mass than a motorbike, and mass is the measure of inertia, so it resists the change in its motion more and needs a greater force or more time to stop.

questions.solution_md: First law and inertia; three kinds with examples; mass measures inertia.

Equal, because the same impulse acts

questions.stem_md: Which of these is the SI unit of momentum?

kg m s⁻²
N m
kg s m⁻¹

questions.solution_md: Momentum is mass times velocity, so its unit is kg × m s⁻¹ = kg m s⁻¹ — option (a). The unit in (b) is the newton.

questions.stem_md: The same net force acts separately on a 2 kg body and a 6 kg body, both starting from rest. The ratio of their accelerations (2 kg body : 6 kg body) is:
questions.solution_md: $a = F/m$, so for the same force $a$ is inversely proportional to $m$: $a_1 : a_2 = 6 : 2 = 3 : 1$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A bullet of mass 0.05 kg moves at 300 m s⁻¹ and a person of mass 60 kg walks at 2 m s⁻¹. Compare their momenta.

The bullet has the greater momentum

questions.stem_md: In a collision the time over which a passenger stops is increased from 0.1 s to 0.5 s by an airbag. The change of momentum is the same. The average force on the passenger becomes:

options.text_md: five times its earlier value
the same as before
zero
one fifth of its earlier value

questions.solution_md: $F = \Delta p / t$, so with the same $\Delta p$ the force is inversely proportional to time. $0.1 / 0.5 = 1/5$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A fast cricket ball is caught first by a fielder with stiff hands and then by another who draws her hands back. For the second fielder the force on her hands is smaller because:

options.text_md: the ball loses less momentum
the ball has a smaller mass
the ball takes longer to stop, so the same change of momentum takes place over a longer time
the ball has a greater speed

questions.solution_md: The change of momentum is the same in both catches. Force $= \Delta p / t$, so a longer stopping time means a smaller force — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The same net force gives a smaller acceleration to a heavier body than to a lighter body.

**Reason (R):** For a given net force, the acceleration of a body is inversely proportional to its mass.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: From $a = F/m$ the acceleration falls as the mass rises, which is exactly what A says. R states this relation, so it explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A fielder draws her hands back while catching a fast ball.

**Reason (R):** The momentum of a body is the product of its mass and its velocity.

Choose the correct option.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.solution_md: A is true and R is true, but R only defines momentum. It does not explain why the hands are drawn back, which is to increase the stopping time and reduce the force — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The momentum of a body is the product of its mass and its ___.
questions.solution_md: Momentum $p = mv$ is mass times **velocity**.

questions.stem_md: A car of mass 1200 kg pulls away from a traffic light with an acceleration of 2.5 m s⁻². Find the net force on the car, in N.
A net force of 24 N gives a trolley an acceleration of 0.80 m s⁻². Find the mass of the trolley, in kg.

A fielder catches a ball of mass 0.15 kg moving at 20 m s⁻¹ and brings it to rest in 0.030 s. Find the average force on her hands, in N.
questions.solution_md: Change of momentum $= 0.15 \times 20 = 3.0\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$. $F = \Delta p / t = 3.0 / 0.03 = 100$ N.

marking_scheme.step: Change of momentum 3.0 kg m s⁻¹

questions.stem_md: A car of mass 1500 kg moving at 20 m s⁻¹ is brought to rest uniformly in 4.0 s. Find the average braking force, in N.
questions.solution_md: $a = (0 - 20) / 4 = -5\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. $F = ma = 1500 \times (-5) = -7500$ N, so the braking force is 7500 N. (Check with $\Delta p / t = 30000 / 4 = 7500$ N.)

marking_scheme.step: Finds a = −5.0 m s⁻² or Δp = 30 000 kg m s⁻¹

questions.stem_md: A steady force of 40 N acts for 0.25 s on a ball of mass 2.0 kg that is initially at rest. Find the speed of the ball afterwards, in m s⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: Impulse $= Ft = 40 \times 0.25 = 10\ \text{N s}$ $= \Delta p = mv$, so $v = 10 / 2 = 5.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: State the second law of motion and use it to define the newton.

answer.model_answer_md: The rate of change of momentum of a body is proportional to the net force on it, and acts in the direction of the force. For constant mass this gives force equal to mass times acceleration. One newton is the force that gives a mass of one kilogram an acceleration of one metre per second squared.

questions.solution_md: Law statement; F = ma; definition of the newton.

questions.stem_md: Athletes in a long-jump event land in a pit of soft sand and not on hard ground. Explain why, using the idea of change of momentum.

answer.model_answer_md: The athlete’s momentum falls to zero on landing, on sand or on hard ground. Soft sand gives way and increases the time taken to stop, so the force on the legs, the change of momentum divided by the time, is much smaller. Hard ground stops the athlete almost at once, giving a large force.

questions.solution_md: Same change of momentum, longer time, smaller force.

marking_scheme.step: Longer time on sand, so F = Δp/t is smaller

questions.stem_md: A body of mass m changes its velocity from u to v in time t under a constant net force F. Starting from the second law in terms of momentum, show that F = ma.

answer.model_answer_md: The initial momentum is $mu$ and the final momentum is $mv$, so the change of momentum is $mv - mu = m(v - u)$. The rate of change of momentum is $\dfrac{m(v - u)}{t}$. By the second law this is proportional to $F$, and with the unit of force chosen as the newton the constant is 1. Since $\dfrac{v - u}{t} = a$, we get $F = ma$.

questions.solution_md: Rate of change of momentum m(v − u)/t = ma.

marking_scheme.step: Rate of change = m(v − u)/t, proportional to F

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define momentum and state its SI unit.

(b) State the second law of motion and show that it gives F = ma.

(c) Why does the same net force produce a smaller acceleration in a heavier body? Support your answer with the graph of acceleration against force for two masses.

answer.model_answer_md: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity, $p = mv$, with unit kg m s⁻¹. The second law states that the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the net force and acts in its direction. For constant mass, the rate of change is $m(v - u)/t = ma$, so $F = ma$. Since $a = F/m$, for a given force the acceleration is inversely proportional to mass. On the graph of acceleration against force, both masses give straight lines through the origin, but the line for the greater mass is less steep, showing a smaller acceleration for the same force.

questions.solution_md: Momentum and unit; second law and F = ma; a = F/m with graph.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Second law and the proof of F = ma
(c) a = F/m, less steep line for the greater mass

questions.stem_md:
A force of 2400 N acts for 5.0 s on a car of mass 800 kg, starting from rest on a smooth level road. Ignore friction.

(a) Find the acceleration of the car.

(b) Find its speed after 5.0 s and its momentum then.

(c) Show that the impulse of the force equals the momentum gained.

answer.model_answer_md: The road is smooth, so the net force on the car is the given force of 2400 N. By the second law, the acceleration of the car is $a = F/m = 2400 / 800 = 3.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Starting from rest, the speed after 5.0 s is $v = at = 3.0 \times 5.0 = 15.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The momentum is $p = mv = 800 \times 15.0 = 12000\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$. The impulse of the force is $Ft = 2400 \times 5.0 = 12000\ \text{N s}$, the same number as the momentum gained. This is expected, because the car started from rest and the impulse of a force equals the change of momentum that it produces in the body.

marking_scheme.step: (b) v = 15 m s⁻¹ and p = 12 000 kg m s⁻¹
(c) Impulse 12 000 N s equals the change of momentum

children.stem_md: Find the average force on the dummy without the airbag, in N.
**Either** (i): Find the average force with the airbag and compare it with the force without the airbag.

questions.stem_md: A book rests on a table. The force of the book pressing down on the table is one force of an action–reaction pair. The other force of the pair is:

options.text_md: the weight of the book acting on the book
the upward push of the table on the book
the downward pull of the Earth on the table
the friction between the book and the table

questions.stem_md: A swimmer moves forward through water by pushing the water backward with her hands. The force that moves her forward is exerted by:

options.text_md: her hands on the water
the Earth on the swimmer
the air above the water
the water on her hands

options.text_md: the exhaust gas pushes against the air
the gas it throws out downward exerts an equal and opposite force upward on the rocket
its weight acts upward in space
the rocket is pulled by the Moon

questions.stem_md: A light girl and a heavier boy stand on smooth ice, face to face and at rest. They push each other apart. Immediately afterwards:

options.text_md: they move with equal and opposite momenta, and the girl has the greater speed
they move with equal speeds in opposite directions
the boy has the greater momentum
only the girl moves

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The action and reaction forces cancel each other, because they are equal in size and opposite in direction.

**Reason (R):** The action and the reaction act on different bodies.

Choose the correct option.

questions.stem_md: A rifle of mass 3.0 kg fires a bullet of mass 0.015 kg at 300 m s⁻¹. Find the recoil speed of the rifle, in m s⁻¹. (The rifle is initially at rest.)
questions.solution_md: Momentum of the bullet $= 0.015 \times 300 = 4.5\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$. The rifle gets an equal momentum backward: $3 \times v = 4.5$, so $v = 4.5 / 3 = 1.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: Two skaters stand at rest on smooth ice and push each other apart. The boy of mass 60 kg moves off at 1.0 m s⁻¹. Find the speed of the girl of mass 40 kg, in m s⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: The momenta are equal and opposite: $40 \times v = 60 \times 1$, so $v = 60 / 40 = 1.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in the opposite direction.

marking_scheme.step: Equal and opposite momenta: 60 × 1.0 = 60 kg m s⁻¹

questions.stem_md: In a tug of war, the rope pulls team A towards team B with a force of 600 N. What force does the rope exert on team B, and what law tells you? Why do the two forces not cancel?

answer.model_answer_md: The rope pulls team B with a force of 600 N in the opposite direction. This follows from Newton’s third law. The two forces do not cancel because they act on different bodies, one on each team, so each team can still move.

questions.solution_md: Third law: equal and opposite; different bodies.

marking_scheme.step: 600 N opposite, by the third law
Act on different bodies so they do not cancel

questions.stem_md: Explain why a gun recoils when it fires a bullet, and why the recoil speed of the gun is much smaller than the speed of the bullet.

answer.model_answer_md: The gun exerts a forward force on the bullet. By the third law the bullet exerts an equal and opposite force on the gun, which makes the gun recoil. The two forces act for the same time, so the momentum gained by the gun is equal and opposite to that of the bullet. The gun has a much greater mass, so for the same momentum its speed is much smaller.

questions.solution_md: Third law gives recoil; equal and opposite momentum; larger mass means smaller speed.

marking_scheme.step: Equal and opposite force on the gun, by the third law

questions.stem_md: Explain, using the third law, how a rocket moves upward. Say why it can also move in the empty space of the sky.

answer.model_answer_md: Burning fuel produces hot gas, and the rocket pushes this gas downward at high speed. By the third law the gas pushes the rocket upward with an equal and opposite force. This force acts on the rocket, which therefore accelerates upward. The reaction comes from the gas itself, not from the air, so the rocket can also move in space where there is no air.

questions.solution_md: Rocket pushes gas down; gas pushes rocket up; no air needed.

marking_scheme.step: Gas pushes the rocket upward, equal and opposite

questions.stem_md: Explain how a person is able to walk forward on the ground using the third law, and say why walking on smooth ice is difficult.

answer.model_answer_md: When we walk, the foot pushes the ground backward. By the third law the ground pushes the foot forward with an equal force, and this reaction moves us ahead. The push on the ground needs friction to grip. On smooth ice the friction is very small, so the foot slips, the reaction is small and walking becomes difficult.

questions.solution_md: Foot pushes ground back; ground pushes forward; ice has little friction.

marking_scheme.step: Ground pushes the foot forward, by the third law
Ice has little friction so the foot slips

questions.stem_md:

(b) Explain how the law works for (i) a swimmer and (ii) a rocket.

answer.model_answer_md: The third law states that to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; the two forces act on different bodies. A swimmer pushes the water backward and the water pushes her forward. A rocket pushes burning gas downward and the gas pushes the rocket upward. For (c), the momentum of the bullet is $0.012 \times 450 = 5.4\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$.
